name: Operation on a Resource after Expiration or Release
principle: Code uses, accesses, or operates on a resource after it has been expired, released, closed, invalidated, or revoked. The stale handle may now refer to invalid state or a different entity, causing crashes, data corruption, or unauthorized data access.
detection_signals: C/C++ pointer passed to dereference, memcpy, strcpy, printf("%s"), or function call after free(ptr)
C++ object pointer/reference used after delete p or delete[] p
same pointer or handle passed to free, delete, fclose, close, or Release more than once
file descriptor used in read, write, send, recv, fcntl, dup, or fdopen after close(fd)
FILE* used in fread, fwrite, fprintf, fflush, or fclose after fclose(fp)
Java object used after close(), e.g. InputStream.read(), Socket.getInputStream(), Channel.write(), or ResultSet.next() after close()
session/token/certificate/key accepted after invalidate(), logout, revocation, or expiration timestamp
negative_signals: resource variable set to NULL or -1 immediately after release and checked before every later use
all uses occur before free, delete, close, fclose, invalidate, revoke, or expiration check failure
ownership transferred with std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr, try-with-resources, or RAII and no raw alias is later used
Java use is inside try-with-resources block and no reference escapes after the block
code reacquires a fresh handle/session/key and uses the new variable after expiration or release
false_defense_traps: checking ptr != NULL after free without assigning ptr = NULL
checking fd >= 0 after close without assigning fd = -1
logging or error handling with a buffer after freeing it
validating expiration only at creation/login while reusing the resource later
non-atomic reference count checks around release in shared or concurrent code
verification_focus: Can any execution path operate on the same resource handle, pointer, session, key, certificate, or descriptor after its release, expiration, invalidation, or revocation?

consequence_chains.trigger: resource is released before its expected lifetime ends
consequence_chains.consequence: later legitimate code uses an expired resource

consequence_chains.trigger: released heap memory is dereferenced through a stale pointer
consequence_chains.consequence: memory corruption, crash, or sensitive data access

consequence_chains.trigger: closed file descriptor integer is reused
consequence_chains.consequence: I/O occurs on the wrong file, socket, or process resource

patch_principle: Move all required operations before release, close, invalidate, revoke, or expiration.
After release, clear the handle to NULL, -1, or an invalid state and guard every use.
Use ownership/lifetime constructs such as RAII, smart pointers, try-with-resources, or scoped handles.
Revalidate expiration or revocation immediately before each security-sensitive use.
Avoid aliases to releasable resources or update all aliases when ownership is transferred.
